opus-5.5.text:
Well, I don't object to it exactly. There *is* a diffusion module in AlphaFold 3, and it's an important change. What I push back on is the idea that diffusion is where the magic happens, because I think that gets the story backwards.

If you look at where the computation and the learning actually live, most of it is in the trunk, the Pairformer, which descends directly from the Evoformer in AlphaFold 2. That's where the model takes in the sequences, the alignments, the templates, the ligands, and builds up this rich pairwise representation of what's near what and how things relate. By the time you get to the diffusion part, a huge amount of the hard inference about the structure has already been done. The diffusion module is, in a sense, a very good way of reading out coordinates from that representation.

So why diffusion at all? In AlphaFold 2 we had a structure module that was quite bespoke. It reasoned in terms of residue frames, backbone and side-chain torsions, all very protein-specific. Once you want to handle arbitrary small molecules, nucleic acids, modified residues, ions, all of that chemistry, the hand-built parameterization becomes a real burden. Diffusion over raw atom coordinates is wonderfully general. You don't need special rules for every chemical species. You let the model learn to denoise atoms, and it handles local stereochemistry very nicely. We could also drop a lot of the complicated losses and equivariance machinery we'd previously needed.

It's also generative, so you can sample multiple outputs, which is useful. But that comes with costs people don't always mention. Generative models will happily hallucinate plausible-looking structure in regions that are really disordered, so we had to do things like cross-distillation from AlphaFold 2 predictions so disordered regions look like the extended ribbons you'd expect, not invented compact structure.

So my worry with the "it's a diffusion model" framing is that it suggests the lesson is "use diffusion and you get AlphaFold." That isn't the lesson. The lesson is the same one it's always been: the data, the evolutionary information, the representation and the trunk architecture, and an enormous amount of careful engineering. Diffusion was the right tool for the output layer of this problem. It's not the reason the problem got solved.

r001.rationale: The response says the “diffusion model” framing wrongly implies diffusion explains AlphaFold 3’s success, and argues that diffusion is only the output-layer tool rather than the reason the problem was solved.

r002.rationale: It discusses AlphaFold 2’s bespoke structure module and the Pairformer’s lineage from the Evoformer, but does not describe a shift from AlphaFold 1 to AlphaFold 2 in where protein-specific science was embedded.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I don't object exactly, but I think it misses the point of what's actually going on. Yes, the structure module at the end of AlphaFold 3 is a diffusion process. We threw away the frame-based structure module from AlphaFold 2 and replaced it with something that takes noisy atomic coordinates and denoises them. That part is true, and it was a big simplification for us because it let us handle arbitrary chemistry, ligands, nucleic acids, modified residues, without having to hand-design a representation for each.

But if you look at where the compute goes, and where the actual biology gets learned, it's in the trunk. The pair representation, the pairformer, the thing that reasons about which residues are near which, which parts of the ligand are interacting with which pocket. That's where the model is doing the hard work of figuring out the structure. The diffusion module is comparatively small and it's largely conditioned on that representation. If you took the trunk away and just had a diffusion model over atom positions, you would get something that looks like a protein but is quite wrong. And conversely, the trunk alone already contains most of the information; the diffusion part is turning that into clean coordinates.

So when people say it's a diffusion model, they tend to import a lot of intuitions from image generation. They think about sampling diversity, about the model being generative in the sense of producing many plausible answers. And that's not really the regime we're in. We want the one right structure. The sampling is useful for giving us a distribution when the biology is genuinely uncertain, and we see that for disordered regions or flexible loops, but mostly we use it as a very good decoder. We even had to deal with the fact that diffusion models will happily hallucinate nice-looking secondary structure in regions that should be disordered, which is a failure mode you inherit from being generative, and we had to train against that.

The other thing I'd say is that the real story of AlphaFold 3 is not an architecture choice, it's the question of generality. Can one model learn the physics of molecular interaction across all these different molecule types rather than one model per problem? The answer turned out to be yes, and diffusion was an enabling tool for that, but it's the tool, not the idea.

r001.rationale: The candidate says calling AlphaFold 3 a diffusion model “misses the point” and argues diffusion is an enabling decoder, while the trunk learns the biology and the key story is generality.

r002.rationale: The candidate compares AlphaFold 2 and 3’s structure modules, but does not describe AlphaFold 1-to-2 as moving protein-specific science from around a generic network into the network’s design.

astra-6.text:
Because that describes one part of the system, and I think it can obscure where a lot of the work is happening. The diffusion model is how we generate the coordinates, but it’s being conditioned on a representation that has already done a tremendous amount of reasoning about the molecules and their interactions.

So if you call it primarily a diffusion model, it sounds as though we took a standard diffusion model, gave it molecular data, and that was the breakthrough. The interesting thing is how the whole system works together: how you represent the problem, how you process the information, and then how you turn that into a structure. Diffusion is an important part of that, but it isn’t the whole explanation.

sol-6.1.text:
Because that describes one part of the architecture, and it can obscure where a lot of the work is happening. The diffusion model is how we generate the coordinates, but it’s conditioned on a representation built by a very substantial network that reasons about the relationships between the atoms and molecules. That representation has to contain the information that makes the structure predictable in the first place.

So I don’t object to saying AlphaFold 3 uses diffusion—it does. I object to treating that as the explanation for why it works. You could attach a diffusion model to a system that doesn’t understand those relationships and you wouldn’t suddenly get accurate molecular structures. The interesting question is how the whole system learns enough about the interactions to generate the right structure.

r001.rationale: The candidate says diffusion describes only coordinate generation and objects to treating it as the explanation for AlphaFold 3’s success; it credits the broader system’s learned molecular relationships.
